_how_to_edit: The story page, replay map and home hero read this file on every load. Edit it, run `node groundstop/src/build.js`, commit and push to main; no Squarespace edit is needed. Times are hours on an Eastern clock on Nov. 13, 2026 (17.5 = 5:30 p.m.; values past 24 mean Nov. 14). Set lift to null while the stop is in effect.
headline_status: The FAA lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. Eastern, after more than four hours
cause: Telecommunications outage on older FAA hardware
moments: A Friday afternoon, with flights departing on schedule across the country.
About 3:10 p.m.
Flights bound for Chicago O’Hare are stopped over communications problems, and Midway follows three minutes later.
Radar and communications at centers and approach facilities across the country become unstable, the transportation secretary says later.
Nationwide ground stop. More than 3,100 flights already in the air are allowed to continue to their destinations.
The transportation secretary says a communication issue is affecting air route traffic control centers.
The FAA advisory now runs to 11:30 p.m. Eastern, and no end time is confirmed.
About 5:15 p.m.
The FAA says a temporary telecommunications outage caused the stop, and officials say they see no sign of an attack.
About 6:00 p.m.
The FAA says the stop remains in effect and that flights will be released as each en route center recovers.
Fox Weather counts 598 commercial flights still in the air, down from more than 3,100 when the stop began.
About 7:10 p.m.
An airline source tells CNN that major airlines could shut down operations for the rest of the night.
FlightAware counts 5,117 cancellations and 9,814 delays, and JetBlue and United call off most of their remaining Friday flights.
The airspace reopens, the transportation secretary says, about 4 hours and 21 minutes after the nationwide stop began.
By 8:48 p.m.
At a White House briefing, the transportation secretary says older hardware failed and that none of the FAA’s new systems went down.
facts: Eastern start time, the only one of the three stops to begin after noon
flights in the air when the stop began, allowed to finish their trips
length of the stop, against about 90 minutes in 2023, with 5,117 flights canceled by 8 p.m. Eastern
unknown: What is not known. The airspace reopened at 8:15 p.m. Eastern, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a White House briefing on Friday night, according to the Department of Transportation. Duffy said switches and routers on older hardware were overloaded with data, beginning at 3:36 p.m., and officials have not said what overloaded them or where the failure began. Three days earlier, on Nov. 10, the agency expanded SMART, an AI tool that suggests flight reroutes, to all 22 centers. Duffy said SMART is not connected to the equipment that failed, according to the Department of Transportation, and the tool’s contractor said the stop was not a result of SMART, according to ABC News.
status_html: The FAA lifted the stop at 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Friday, about 4 hours and 21 minutes after it began. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy gave the time at a White House briefing, saying, “At 8:15 tonight, Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” according to the Department of Transportation. Flying will take longer to recover than the stop took to end, because JetBlue canceled all of its remaining Friday flights except Europe-bound departures from New York and Boston, United said it would cancel most of its remaining flights for the night, and Air Canada canceled the rest of its Friday flights to and from the United States. After the stop was lifted, United said it was “resuming operations, including some planned Friday night flights,” according to ABC News. FlightAware had counted 5,117 cancellations and 9,814 delays by 8 p.m., according to CNN, which is about twice the 2,500 cancellations counted at 6:30 p.m. More than 700 Saturday flights were already canceled by 7:45 p.m., and the data firm Cirium estimated that 1.5 million people were stranded. Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a White House briefing on Friday night that schedules would take a while to recover, with most planes likely to get going on Saturday morning, according to Deadline.
compare_html: Friday's stop lasted about 261 minutes, close to three times the roughly 90 minutes of 2023, and it began late on a Friday afternoon where the 2023 stop began early on a Wednesday, which left airlines almost none of the day to recover. The 5,117 cancellations counted by 8 p.m. were nearly four times the 1,300-plus logged for the whole day in 2023, while the 9,814 delays were about level with that day's roughly 10,000. Cirium counted 26,284 flights scheduled to depart the United States on Friday and said more than 15% were canceled or never took off, and at least 827 flights were diverted, 670 of them back to the airport they left. The effects reach into Saturday: the Big 12 told CNN it is evaluating changes to its football schedule because teams could not travel.
notknown_html:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy gave the first official account of the cause at a White House briefing on Friday night. ABC News reported that he blamed overloaded routers, and Deadline quoted him describing a radar “instability” problem and saying, “It was the old hardware that went down,” and that “none of the new systems went down.” Duffy said the instability in radar and communications began at 3:36 p.m. Eastern, 18 minutes before the nationwide stop, according to the Department of Transportation’s account of the briefing. Officials have not said what overloaded the routers, where the failure began or why it spread to all 22 centers.

Several accounts go further than officials have. An airline source told CNN that the FAA told airlines the outages resulted from a problem with network routers, and that the problem is believed to have started at Chicago Midway and spread nationwide. CBS News reported that an update to the private communications network linking air traffic control facilities caused the system to reboot, and that the network is operated by the contractor L3Harris, which had not responded to its request for comment. The FAA has confirmed none of these details.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a threat to the country, and the FAA said it does not believe the outage was a cyberattack. Mullin said at the briefing that officials had seen “zero evidence” of a cyberattack, according to Deadline, which reported that he would not rule one out. A senior security source told CNN late Friday that the FBI, the Department of Homeland Security and the National Security Agency had found no sign of an attack and that the search of the aviation system’s network connections would continue for days.

Three days before the stop, on Nov. 10, the FAA expanded SMART, an AI tool that suggests flight reroutes, to all 22 centers. Mullin said the administration is examining that rollout, according to Fox News. Duffy said at the briefing that SMART “is completely disconnected” from the equipment that failed and that “there’s no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened,” according to the Department of Transportation. The tool’s contractor said in a statement that the ground stop “is not based on or a result of the SMART system,” according to ABC News, and no official or major outlet has reported a link.

This story reflects what was known at 1:05 a.m. Eastern on Nov. 14, 2026. The lift time is the one Duffy gave at the briefing, and we will update the cause and the final delay and cancellation counts as the FAA and flight trackers report them.
